title: Universality should be common, including among very simple rules

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Universality should be common, including among very simple rules

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The universality of rule 110, one of the simplest possible cellular automaton rules, implies that universality is far more common than previously thought and should occur in a very wide range of systems, including many with rather simple rules.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But knowing that a system like rule 110 is universal, the whole picture changes, and now it seems likely that instead universality should actually be seen in a very wide range of systems, including many with rather simple rules.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 11, “The Notion of Computation”; section “The Significance of Universality in Rule 110” (from p. 690), p. 690. Scope: simple programs of all kinds

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch11-15: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.39

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing enumerations permit informative surveys in finite rule spaces. They cannot resolve the extrapolation to a very wide range of all simple systems, and non-discovery of proofs does not establish nonuniversality.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Predefine system families, a rule-description complexity measure, and universality criteria, then estimate the fraction of universal members by proof or bounded emulation searches. High fractions across multiple low-complexity families would support the restricted prevalence claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Universality is generally undecidable.

There is no canonical measure or sampling distribution over 'systems of all kinds'.

fields.value:

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Rule 110 and a handful of other simple systems are known to be universal, so the prediction can be probed inside small families. Most simple rules are still unclassified, and there is no measure under which an overwhelming share of simple rules has been shown universal. Existing proofs therefore test a sample, not the claim that universality is common across simple programs.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Choose explicit simplicity bounds, such as elementary cellular automata or Turing machines with a bounded state-symbol product, and compute the fraction with a finished universality proof or a finished non-universality proof. The prediction is supported if that fraction is high inside several families, and weakened if proofs keep universality rare among simple rules.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Common, wide range, and rather simple are not given numerical boundaries.

Failure to prove universality is not evidence of non-universality.
